title: Kumarakom Responsible Tourism Model
subtitle: How a destination-level partnership linked tourism demand with local livelihoods, culture and conservation.
audience: Training deck for District & Mandal Level Officials, Andhra Pradesh
source_note: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

sections.title: Why Kumarakom needed a new approach
sections.lead: Tourism growth was strong, but local communities were not fully integrated into benefits and decisions.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

blocks.title: Core challenge
items: Top-down tourism planning with limited community voice
Conflicts over resource use, employment and benefit sharing
Leakage of tourism spending outside the local economy
Need to conserve fragile backwater ecosystems and local culture

blocks.label: Case question for officials
blocks.text: How can mandals convert tourism footfall into local income without damaging natural and cultural assets?

sections.title: Institutional model: a destination-level platform
sections.lead: A Responsible Tourism Committee brought local government, industry and community together.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

blocks.label: Responsible Tourism Committee
blocks.text: A shared governance platform at destination level

blocks.label: Design principle
blocks.text: put government, industry and community in one recurring forum so decisions on tourism products, benefits and safeguards are made jointly.

sections.title: Strategy 1: Link hotel demand with local supply
sections.lead: Local procurement became the economic engine of the model.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

items.title: Production calendar
items.body: When local supply can meet demand

blocks.label: Key learning
blocks.text: Do not start with tourist packages alone. Start by organising the local supply chain so community members can reliably serve tourism demand.

sections.title: Strategy 2: Build community livelihoods around visitor experience
sections.lead: The model diversified income by converting local skills, food and culture into tourism services.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

items.desc: Map skills and local workers for hotel jobs and services
Use local recipes, crafts and SHG production
Package farming, fishing, crafts and local livelihoods as authentic experiences

blocks.label: Replicable insight for AP
blocks.text: Build one local experience around each mandal's strongest asset: agriculture, crafts, cuisine, temples, coastal livelihoods, tribal culture, nature trails or wetlands.

sections.title: Strategy 3: Protect the assets that attract tourists
sections.lead: Kumarakom treated conservation, sanitation and cultural mapping as part of tourism management.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

groups.name: Ecosystem care
items: Fish farming / lotus in unused ponds

blocks.label: Key learning
blocks.text: Tourism plans must include environmental safeguards and cultural preservation from day one—not as a later add-on.

sections.title: Results achieved: measurable economic and social impact
sections.lead: The model increased local income, enterprise creation, cultivation and tourist arrivals.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

sections.title: Key lessons for district and mandal officials
sections.lead: What made the model work—and what should be replicated carefully.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

items.title: Local government must anchor the platform
items.body: Mandal/district administration gives legitimacy and continuity.

items.title: Private sector concerns need practical solutions
items.body: Price, quality and reliability committees make procurement possible.

items.title: Community confidence has to be built
items.body: Use regular hotel-community interactions, exposure visits and transparent processes.

items.title: Capacity building must be demand-led
items.body: Train people in skills linked to actual hotel/visitor demand.

items.title: Destination assets must be protected
items.body: Tourism income depends on wetlands, beaches, culture, cleanliness and trust.

blocks.label: Training prompt
blocks.text: Which 2–3 assets in your mandal can be converted into community-led tourism products without overuse?

sections.title: Replication strategy for Andhra Pradesh
sections.lead: A practical sequence district and mandal teams can adapt to local tourism assets.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

items.title: Identify tourism anchors
items.body: Map beaches, temples, crafts, food, wetlands, hills, tribal circuits and agri-tourism points.

items.title: Create a destination task force
items.body: Include Mandal Parishad, Gram Panchayat, Tourism, DRDA/SHGs, hotels, transporters, youth and artisans.

items.title: Map local supply and skills
items.body: List farmers, fishers, SHGs, artisans, cooks, guides and available facilities.

items.title: Match supply with demand
items.body: Run structured discussions with hotels/tour operators to define price, quality, quantity and delivery.

items.title: Pilot and monitor
items.body: Launch 1–2 low-risk experiences and procurement linkages; track income, participation, cleanliness and visitor feedback.

blocks.text: Replicate the principles, not the exact product: coastal mandals may focus on fishing/boat experiences; temple towns on local food, crafts and heritage walks; tribal/hill mandals on guided nature and culture routes.

sections.title: 90-day action plan and monitoring metrics
sections.lead: Use the case study to move from awareness to a small, visible pilot.
sections.source: Source: NITI for States Best Practice ID 101989; UNWTO Tourism for Development, Vol. II, Case Study 9.

groups.label: 0–15 days
groups.name: Asset & stakeholder mapping
tasks: Tourism assets, hotels, SHGs, producers, existing schemes

groups.label: 15–30 days
groups.name: Task force + MoU structure
tasks: Roles, meeting rhythm, price/quality norms, grievance loop

groups.label: 30–60 days
groups.name: Capacity building + supply groups
tasks: Guide training, food/craft hygiene, production calendars

blocks.title: Suggested monitoring metrics
items: No. of tourists using local experiences

blocks.label: Closing activity
blocks.text: Each official identifies one pilot destination, one community group and one private-sector partner to begin with.
